==Problem==
In a mathematics contest with ten problems, a student gains 5 points for a correct answer and loses 2 points for an incorrect answer. If Olivia answered every problem and her score was 29, how many correct answers did she have?

<math> \text{(A)}\ 5\qquad\text{(B)}\ 6\qquad\text{(C)}\ 7\qquad\text{(D)}\ 8\qquad\text{(E)}\ 9 </math>

==Solution 1==
We can try to guess and check to find the answer. If she got five right, her score would be <math>(5*5)-(5*2)=15</math>. If she got six right her score would be <math>(6*5)-(2*4)=22</math>. That's close, but it's still not right! If she got 7 right, her score would be <math>(7*5)-(2*3)=29</math>. Thus, our answer is <math>\boxed{\text{(C)}\ 7}</math>. ~avamarora

==Solution 2==
We can start with the full score, 50, and subtract not only 2 points for each incorrect answer but also the 5 points we gave her credit for. This expression is equivalent to her score, 29. 
Let <math>x</math> be the number of questions she answers correctly. Then, we will represent the number incorrect by <math>10-x</math>.

<cmath>\begin{align*}
50-7(10-x)&=29\\
50-70+7x&=29\\
7x&=49\\
x&=\boxed{\text{(C)}\ 7}
\end{align*}</cmath>

==Solution 3==
Suppose she got <math>x</math> questions right. Then she got <math>10 - x</math> questions wrong. Since she gains 5 points for a correct answer and loses 2 for an incorrect one, we can solve <math>5x - 2(10 - x) = 29</math> to get that <math>x = \boxed{\text{(C)}\ 7}</math>.

~[https://artofproblemsolving.com/wiki/index.php/User:Cxsmi cxsmi]

==Solution 4==
We see that Olivia's score is odd. Since subtracting multiples of <imath>2</imath> (even numbers) does not change a number's parity (odd or even), Olivia's score from only her correct answers must be odd. Then, we test odd multiples of <imath>5</imath> greater than <imath>29</imath> to see which one works. The smallest odd multiple of <imath>5</imath> greater than <imath>29</imath> is <imath>35</imath>, meaning <imath>7</imath> answers were correct and the remaining <imath>3</imath> answers were wrong. We see that the final score is
<cmath>7(5)-3(2)=35-6=29,</cmath>
which is the score Olivia got. Thus, the answer is <imath>\boxed{(C) 7}</imath>.

==Solution 5==

Suppose <imath>x</imath> represents the number of correctly answered questions and <imath>y</imath> represents the number of incorrectly answered questions.

We can model the situation with the following system of equations:
<cmath>
\begin{cases}
x + y = 10 \\
5x - 2y = 29
\end{cases}
</cmath>

Multiply the first equation by <imath>2</imath> to get:
<cmath>
2x + 2y = 20
</cmath>

Now add this equation to the second equation:
<cmath>
(2x + 2y) + (5x - 2y) = 20 + 29
</cmath>
<cmath>
7x = 49
</cmath>

Solve for <imath>x</imath>:
<cmath>
x = 7
</cmath>

-N.
